title: Unitary complexity in polynomial space
abstract: We show that if quantum commitments exist, then either there is no polynomial-time solution to the unitary synthesis problem, or $\mathsf{BPP} \neq \mathsf{NEXP}$. Thus, showing unconditionally that quantum commitments exist would require answering at least one of two longstanding open questions in complexity theory. We prove our main result as a consequence of a more general lemma, which shows that every unitary in $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ either cannot be synthesized efficiently relative to any classical oracle, or can be synthesized efficiently with an oracle for $\mathsf{NEXP}$ search problems. Our lemma has other noteworthy consequences, including that certain oracle separations involving $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ would imply breakthrough classical lower bounds such as $\mathsf{NC} \neq \mathsf{NP}$.   Along the way, we propose new definitions for the unitary complexity classes $\mathsf{unitaryP}$ and $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$. Our changes address the biggest conceptual issues with definitions suggested in prior work, and lead to elegant proofs. We study both implementations that erase garbage and implementations that allow it, because we cannot rule out the possibility that the two definitions differ. Nevertheless, we show that both definitions can be viewed as special cases of each other. We also showcase many other ways in which our definitions are robust. For example, we show that $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ has an equivalent characterization as the set of unitary transformations whose entries can be computed to arbitrary precision in polynomial space. Consequently, we deduce that $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ can generically erase garbage, a result that provably fails relative to unitary oracles.
summary: This paper explores the computational limits of quantum computation by analyzing the complexity class associated with unitary transformations. It establishes a strong link between the existence of quantum commitments and major open problems in complexity theory, such as whether $	ext{BPP} = 	ext{NEXP}$. The findings refine the understanding of unitary complexity classes and their relationship to classical computational power.
main_problem: The paper investigates the computational hardness of the unitary synthesis problem and relates the existence of quantum commitments to fundamental separations in classical complexity theory.
main_result: The authors prove that if quantum commitments exist, then either the unitary synthesis problem has no polynomial-time solution, or the complexity classes BPP and NEXP are unequal.
method: The work employs advanced complexity theory, defining new unitary complexity classes (unitaryP, unitaryPSPACE) and using general lemmas to connect the computational power of these classes to known classical separations.
model_or_system: The theoretical model centers on unitary transformations ($U$) and the associated complexity classes ($	ext{unitaryP}$, $	ext{unitaryPSPACE}$), abstracting away from specific physical hardware.
key_observables: The primary observables are the relationships between complexity classes ($	ext{unitaryP}$ vs $	ext{unitaryPSPACE}$) and the existence of quantum commitments (EFI pairs).
important_parameters: The key parameters are the computational resources: polynomial time, polynomial space, and the separation between $	ext{BPP}$ and $	ext{NEXP}$.
main_assumptions: The main assumption is the hypothetical existence of quantum commitments, which serves as the trigger for the complexity implications.
paper_structure: The paper introduces refined definitions for unitary complexity classes, proves a main theorem linking quantum commitments to complexity separations, and develops supporting lemmas relating $	ext{unitaryPSPACE}$ to efficient synthesis or $	ext{NEXP}$ search problems.
why_interesting: This work provides deep theoretical constraints on what can be computed unitarily, linking fundamental questions in quantum computation (like commitment schemes) directly to the hierarchy of classical complexity classes.
